1:
Where the chapter stands is settled by what it assumes. Keil and Delitzsch date it to Hezekiah's earliest years, since Samaria has not yet fallen, and set the chapters that follow against the preceding ones as a mirror of two reigns: the earlier marked by spiritless submission to the Assyrian yoke, this one by a striving after liberty, the people throwing the yoke off not in confidence toward God but in reliance on Egypt, a policy traced here step by step. Charles Ellicott finds it remarkable for another reason, that the prophet's work was not confined to Judah and Jerusalem but reached the northern kingdom; the warning was uttered before the capital fell, and it paints the licence that capital had sunk into, with a side glance at the same vices nearer home. Adam Clarke lays out the plan: a denunciation of the northern ruin, then a turn to the two tribes who were to continue after their brethren's captivity, then reproofs for intemperance and profaneness. John Calvin marks it off as a new subject: the vengeance of God falls first on Israel and afterwards on the Jews.

The crown and the valley are read together. Ellicott sees a bold personification working twice, first the banquet with its revellers wearing wreaths of flowers as the Romans later did, then Samaria itself as such a wreath, once beautiful and now fading, crowning the head of the valley. Matthew Henry supplies the setting: Ephraim took his name from fruitfulness, and Samaria, seated on a hill, stood as on the head of the fat valleys, the country pleasant as the garden of the Lord and its harvest and vintage the glorious beauty. John Wesley gives it in short, a proud kingdom whose many excellent vines exposed it to the sin charged against it.

Whether the mighty one who overthrows them is a person or a thing divides them. Delitzsch renders the phrase neuter, a strong and mighty thing held ready like a hailstorm. Calvin knows the reading that makes it the Assyrians but prefers to take it without a substantive, as a staff or other instrument by which the Lord will cast down this pride, keeping the flower of the opening verse in view, since nothing is more destructive to flowers than hail. Ellicott allows the Hebrew to be neuter, with the Greek and Targum, or masculine, with our version, and says either way it points to the Assyrian king. Gill and Wesley name that king outright. Clarke construes the words as a Hebraism for the exceedingly strong one, and reports that many manuscripts read the divine name where our text has Lord.

Clarke would read crowns in the plural to agree with its verb, and Wesley draws out that verb's force: the crown on their own heads shall be trodden under the feet of others, and men whose drunkenness had brought them to the ground shall be trodden down there.

The fig at the end draws the tile's fullest comment. Clarke quotes a traveller on the tree's three crops: no sooner does the early fig approach perfection about midsummer than the summer fig begins to form, and the same tree often throws a third, longer and darker, ripening after the leaves are shed and gathered as a delicious morsel in spring. Ellicott takes the first as the point, a delicacy that becomes a type of the doomed city's pride; the passer-by seizes such a fig and devours it at once, and so, with a homeliness he calls worthy of Dante, the Assyrian king would deal with Samaria. Calvin explains why the prophet says almost the same thing twice: it is hard to terrify men blinded by prosperity, and he adds the example of a tyrant so gorged at unseasonable banquets that he stumbled constantly, pleasures blinding men until they know neither God nor themselves.
5:
Here the prophecy changes its object, and everyone marks the turn. Adam Clarke says it has so far related to the Israelites and now turns to the two tribes, opening with a favourable prognostication that soon changes to reproof. Charles Ellicott sets the crown of glory in direct contrast with the crown of pride just trampled, and finds an earnest of the promise in the gathering of some northern tribes at the king's passover. John Gill takes the crown as surrounding and protecting a people to whom God gives large measures of grace, and dates it to the year the ten tribes were carried away.

Two narrow the promise. John Calvin will not extend it indiscriminately to all the Jews but only to the elect wonderfully rescued from death, and draws the rule that the Church is never so disfigured that the Lord does not adorn it. Matthew Henry narrows it differently, to those who glory in the Lord of hosts himself, adding that only in Christ does a holy God communicate with sinful man. Clarke reports that the ancient Aramaic paraphrase read the verse of the Messiah outright.

The gifts named next are read as the two halves of good government. Calvin says the art of civil government consists of counsel within and strength against enemies without, and that God gives both. Ellicott hears an echo of the spiritual gifts listed earlier in the book, notes that corrupt judges were the crying evil of both capitals, and takes the brave men set beside the upright judges as those who drive the enemy back to the gate he came out of, or beat him at the gate he attacks. Clarke prefers the first, the war carried to the enemy's own gate.

The reproof begins abruptly, and the abruptness is the point. Keil and Delitzsch note that with the words and they also the prophet opens the address's second half and passes from the northern kingdom to Judah. Ellicott hears the method of the prophet who said thou art the man: having painted the drunkards of one capital, he paints those of the other in darker colours still, priests reeling to their services and prophets reeling in the very act of their counterfeit inspiration, the word for reeling repeated three times to press the scandal home. John Wesley says Judah is guilty of the same sins and must expect the same calamities, the prophets miscarrying in their sacred employment while the priests mistake in pronouncing the sentence of the law.

Whether the drink is literal is the one real division. Gill, Ellicott and Wesley take it as it stands, a vice common to every rank, so the people could hardly be blamed for following. Calvin takes the wine and strong drink metaphorically and reads a charge of aggravated ingratitude: these men had a striking proof of God's anger before their eyes in their brethren's chastisement while experiencing his forbearance toward themselves, and neither severity nor goodness could bring them back.

On the fouled tables they agree, and are unsparing. Gill distinguishes the two words, one for what a loaded stomach throws up and the other for what the body voids, both giving a just though nauseous idea of a drunken man; the tables meant are those of the priests who ate the holy things and of the prophets who pretended to see visions. Calvin keeps the picture and draws the moral, that men given to drunkenness forget shame, debase themselves below beasts and shrink from nothing disgraceful, so the figure describes the whole life of the people as shameful beyond endurance and says in a word that no uprightness was left. Delitzsch carries the scene into the sneer that follows, the hearers treating the prophet as an intolerable moralist and answering that they are of age and free.
9:
Whose voice speaks these verses is the question everything turns on. Adam Clarke has the scoffers uttering their own sententious speeches and treating God's warnings with derision: does he treat us as infants just weaned, perpetually inculcating the same elementary lessons? Their mockery ridicules the prophet's own concise manner, and God then retorts with great severity. Charles Ellicott reads them the same way, as the drunkards talking scornfully of a man who comes to them with what he calls his knowledge as though they were boys fit for an infant school; the iteration they ascribe to him is puerile harping on one note, and he can scarcely doubt the prophet was reproducing their words.

The rest take the words as the prophet's own. John Gill asks whom such a teacher can instruct in the knowledge of God and the way of salvation. Matthew Henry complains of the wretched stupidity of a people unteachable and making no improvement of the means of grace they had, since it is God's way to enlighten the mind with his truth and so gain the affections. John Calvin turns it into amazement that the disease is incurable: calling wanderers back and unceasingly warning those who stray is itself an extraordinary remedy, so if it does no good the case of men who refuse all help is hopeless. John Wesley reduces it to a sentence: a minister may as soon teach an infant as these men.

The repeated formula draws grammar from one and pedagogy from the rest. Clarke calls the original remarkably abrupt and explains its two nouns: the first a diminutive suited to a child's capacity, used so nowhere else, the second the mason's line stretched to build a course of stones by, raised again for each layer. Calvin makes it a schoolroom where the master spends a whole day on a single letter and must renew the labour next day, nothing that care can do making the pupils improve. Gill compares a child given one rule of a language after another.

The stammering tongue is the second dispute. Ellicott makes it the Assyrian conquerors, whose speech would strike the men of Judah as a barbarous patois and who with their short sharp commands would next utter God's will to a people that would not hear the prophet. Wesley says the same, a people of strange language brought among them because they would not hear God in their own. Keil and Delitzsch take the connecting word out of the scoffers' mouths and carry it on in the prophet's, ungodliness of that kind meeting an appropriate punishment.

Calvin refers the stammering to God himself, who became a barbarian to a people without understanding, and thinks the reproof must have wounded them to the quick, since by their own fault they made the God who formed our tongues appear a stammerer; the verse does not yet threaten but lays the blame on their indolence in turning the proclamation of heavenly doctrine into a confused noise. Gill will have it either way, as the lisping by which parents accommodate a child's weakness, or as the rougher speech of an invading people.

The offer they refused is stated plainly. Ellicott has the prophet vindicating himself against the charge of endlessly repeating rebuke, since he had pointed the way to repentance and so to rest, and to this too they closed their ears; they had one formula of derision whatever he taught, and he repeats it back with all the scorn of irony. Calvin rejects as feeble the reading that turns the clause into a supposition; the prophet is rather giving the reason why God seemed to them a barbarian, which is that they had no ears, and their wickedness was doubly inexcusable in refusing a rest all men naturally desire. Wesley makes the rest the doctrine itself, the only way in which they would find any.
14:
The scorners are identified before they are answered. Charles Ellicott presses the closing words and finds the men who derided the prophet among the king's own princes and counsellors, partisans now of an Assyrian and now of an Egyptian alliance, anything rather than a policy of righteousness. Matthew Henry marks the escalation: having reproved those who made a jest of the word of God, the prophet turns on those who made a jest of his judgments, and observes how bad it is with a people when the thrones of judgment become the seats of the scornful. John Calvin defines the name: men addicted to sophistry and deceit who suppose that by jeers and cunning they can escape God's judgment; and the address is not to ordinary men but to rulers who thought they surpassed everyone else in sharpness.

Their boast is proverbial, and two of them can produce the proverb. Adam Clarke explains that to be in covenant with a thing was a common way of saying one was safe from it, and finds a close parallel in the Roman poet's account of a tribe unhurt by serpents. Ellicott agrees the phrase was proverbial, notes that the second term is the Hebrew word for the region of the dead, and hears in the clause about the overflowing scourge a sneer at the prophet's own imagery, since he had painted the invasion first as a flood and then as a scourge, and the scorners reckon their lies will shelter them under either figure.

What they were actually relying on is put three ways. Calvin says they promised themselves escape in the middle of their crimes and grew bolder for it, since by ridiculing all God's threatenings they supposed themselves out of danger. John Wesley makes the lying and dissimulation itself their security, and John Gill has them thinking it rather than saying it, their conduct showing the sentiments of their minds. Keil and Delitzsch set the verses out as one movement.

The stone is where the tile turns, and Ellicott separates two questions usually run together. First the imagery: ancient architecture attached the same importance to a foundation stone that modern does, and in Zion that stone was laid on the solid rock, as the Arabic name of the building now standing there testifies. Then the interpretation: from the prophet's own standpoint this was identical with the manifestation of God's righteousness in and through the temple.

The others go straight to the person. Clarke reports that one rabbi understood the verse of the king then reigning, but says it belongs to Jesus Christ alone, and that even the Jews could not contest his application of it to himself. Henry calls it a promise of Christ as the only foundation of hope for escaping the wrath to come, laid in Zion in the eternal counsels of God, a tried stone that never failed anyone who made trial of it. Wesley works through the epithets: the Messiah, tried and approved as every way sufficient, uniting the parts of the building. Gill explains why the promise stands in the middle of a denunciation: the godly, hearing the sentence, might conclude the nation was to be cut off and the house of David ended, and then ask where the promise of the Messiah was.

Calvin takes the comfort rather than the identification. The godly were a laughingstock to these crafty men, as irreligious men still laugh at what they take for simplicity and reckon believers fools for hoping, amid deep adversity, that things will turn out well; against that insolence the prophet tells them to pass the jeers by and hold firmly that their hope will not be confounded. Wesley draws the practical edge from the last clause, that the man who believes will not hastily catch at any way of escaping danger but will wait patiently upon God.
17:
The builder's tools that open the passage are read two ways. Charles Ellicott renders the clause that judgment is made a line and righteousness a plummet, and continues the architecture: the elect corner stone comes up to the standard of perfection and is the true refuge, while the scorners' boast proves false and their shelter is swept away by the great waters. John Calvin reads it as a promise that God has the means ready to form the Church anew, so there is no reason to fear he will leave the building unfinished, though the words indirectly reprove men who wished to be counted pillars of that Church while pulling it down. John Wesley turns the tools the other way: a plumb-line serves not only in raising a building but in taking one down, marking the parts to be demolished.

The undoing of the covenant produces a nice question about a word. John Gill notes that the term for disannulled properly means besmeared or daubed over, the word used of the pitching of the ark, so the covenant is blotted like writing spoiled by ink until its articles cannot be made out. Adam Clarke thinks the word does not belong here and prefers the Chaldee's reading, approved by two scholars.

On the relentlessness of what comes they agree. Ellicott has the dread rumours of the Assyrian march arriving day by day, so the report that had been unintelligible becomes plain, and instead of line upon line there is mourning upon mourning, each morning bringing its alarming tidings, until to understand them is itself a terror. Wesley says the scourge will not merely come but abide, and having passed over will return morning after morning without the least respite, so dreadful that the rumour alone strikes horror. Calvin explains the state of mind it interrupts: wicked men do perceive they are liable to calamities, but stupefy themselves with proverbs about not distressing oneself before the time and enjoying the season while it lasts.

The proverb of the bed is the tile's best-handled image. Clarke calls it a saying meaning that every means of defence will prove insufficient, notes that the word for covering serves elsewhere for the outworks that form a country's barrier, and describes the furniture: beds were mattresses on the floor and the coverlet a sheet, or in winter a carpet a man wrapped himself in. Ellicott applies it to the politics, the counsellors having made their bed and having to lie on it in their Egyptian alliance, bed and blankets alike too scanty and leaving them in restless disquietude. Calvin makes it torture rather than discomfort: they are shut into a short and narrow bed where they can scarcely stretch a limb or lift the head, so the thing given for rest becomes an instrument of pain.

The strange work is explained by the two battles named beside it. Ellicott points out that at both God had interposed on behalf of his people against their enemies, and that the new and strange thing, the very paradox of prophecy, is that he should now rise up to overthrow his own people. Wesley says the same from the other side, that bringing total destruction on Israel was contrary to the benignity of God's own nature and to his usual way of dealing with them. Gill recalls that the Lord broke forth on David's enemies there as a breach of waters, whence the place got its name.

The warning at the close leaves a door open. Delitzsch observes that repentance was still possible and at least a modification of the threat attainable, the assumption being that they are already in fetters which their mockery would only make stronger. Gill remarks how natural such mockery is when judgment is deferred, and that it was one cause of the ruin that came.
23:
Why the chapter ends in a parable is answered four ways. Keil and Delitzsch say an ingredient is still wanting to balance the first half, since the prophet must comfort the believers who make themselves his disciples as well as alarm the scoffers. Adam Clarke has him close a discourse of severe reproof with a defence of God's method, in an allegory drawn wholly from agriculture. Charles Ellicott notes that the parable is set before them uninterpreted, and finds its root idea in men's failure to bring to the signs of the times the wisdom they use readily in tillage. John Calvin observes the mismatch between so weighty a preface and so ordinary a subject, and says the prophet meant to lift his hearers higher, showing with what wisdom God governs a world wicked men think moves by chance. Matthew Henry compares it to the Gospel parables and keeps the plain sense, the husbandman going about his calling with pains and prudence.

The ploughing is where the application is fixed. Ellicott makes it the preparatory discipline that fits the spiritual soil for the sower, a means and not an end and so only for a season; to a nation watching Assyrian invaders score their furrows across the land, it held out hope of a harvest. John Gill says the ploughman ploughs in order to sow, and may plough a whole day but not every day; the Lord likewise is not always at one task. John Wesley draws the rebuke from it, that God has his times and seasons and the scoffers flattered themselves foolishly on his long patience, since he will take a time to thresh them.

Calvin sets himself against the received reading. It is commonly explained as if the Lord reproached his people for ingratitude, having cultivated the field with all his care and reaped nothing worth having; but the prophet's meaning connects rather with what he had said of the destruction revealed to him, that God does not always display his hand in one way.

The sowing is measured, and the seeds are disputed. Calvin has the sower measure the ground rather than throw in all he can, and takes the disputed word to mean in measure rather than excellent. Ellicott calls the passage an excerpt from the Georgics of Palestine, and follows a modern scholar in reading fennel seed where our version gives fitches. Wesley keeps the plainer sense, the best grain chosen for seed, each kind in its place.

That the skill is taught is the parable's hinge. Ellicott makes the point without mythology: the tiller's skill, which looks like the fruit of long experience, is nothing less than a gift of God, where Gentile legends wrapped the same truth in myths. Calvin presses an argument from the less to the greater: if men are so well taught in small matters, will the teacher himself not know when to cut down a people and what chastisement suits each?

The threshing carries the discrimination to the end. Adam Clarke distinguishes four instruments: the flail for tenderer grain, the drag of rough planks studded with stones and drawn over the sheaves, the wheeled wain, and the treading of cattle. Ellicott says a man would be thought mad who threshed the smallest seeds with the instrument used for wheat, and reads the gentler tools of the little ones of the earth, whom God handles more tenderly. He turns the last verse into a question, whether bread corn is crushed to pieces, and answers that as the poor were the small seeds, Israel in its greatness was the bread corn needing a severer threshing; but the end of threshing is to preserve the true grain, and the wheels stop when their work is done. Clarke closes on the text, restoring a conjunction on two versions' authority and reading hoofs for horsemen, words that differ by a single letter.
